title: POC Scope: Performance SLO Playbook (TTFT vs TPOT) - BrightScale
topics: Define TTFT vs TPOT for BrightScale workloads
Workload sizing and synthetic benchmark plan
Measurement methodology: warm vs cold cache
Timeline and responsibilities for POC run
summary: Redwood AE + SE aligned with BrightScale on defining production SLOs: use TTFT for interactive first-response constraints and TPOT for sustained token throughput; agreed on p95/p99 targets, a staged benchmark plan (baseline, scaled, burst), and a 3-week POC timeline with specific artifacts to share.

BrightScale to provide representative prompt corpus + traffic distribution (by 2025-05-26)
Connor to propose exact instance sizing and RBI (recommended batch sizes / KV cache tests) (by 2025-05-27)
action_items: Maya - upload Redwood benchmark harness + instructions - due 2025-05-24
Leah - export 3 days of anonymized request traces + token histograms - due 2025-05-26

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-05-22 | Time: 15:30 PT | Duration: ~58m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Carlos (CTO, BrightScale), Leah (ML Eng), Sofia (Infra)
Links shared: https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/brightscale-poc (demo harness placeholder), security doc link (sent after)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. quick intro, i'm maya, i'm the account lead on this POC. Connor is our SE who will run the bench side. How's everybody doing?
[00:12] Carlos: good, thanks. we've been trying to get clarity on realtime latency vs throughput for our chat endpoint. want to make sure our SLOs are realistic before we commit to dedicated capacity.
[00:23] Maya: totally. the call goal is to pick clear SLOs — TTFT vs TPOT — and a measurement plan so both teams can run the same tests. also agree an acceptance criteria for the POC.
[00:34] Connor: quick defs from our side: TTFT = time to first token, it matters for interactive UX. TPOT = time per output token (we sometimes call it tokens/sec inversion), which captures sustained throughput. we'll also look at aggregate throughput (reqs/sec) for steady-state.
[00:50] Leah: can you explain difference in practice? like when TTFT is more important than TPOT?
[00:55] Connor: yeah — TTFT drives perceived responsiveness, so for a customer-facing chat it's a primary metric (p95 or p99). TPOT matters when you stream long responses or have high-concurrency batches; it drives cost and overall capacity planning.
[01:15] Carlos: ok. our baseline target is "snappy" — product team suggested p95 below 150ms for first token for short replies. but that was a ballpark. we need redwood to help set something engineering-safe.
[01:30] Maya: understood. typical Redwood baseline we see: TTFT p95 in 80-200ms range depending on model and infra; TPOT p95 can be 10-40ms per token depending on quantization and batch sizes. we should pick specific numbers tied to BrightScale profile.
[01:47] Sofia: important to call out: our infra runs in GCP us-west and we need a VPC peering for private POC. timing wise we have a maintenance window for peering next Thursday.
[01:58] Connor: cool. for the POC we'll run three phases: baseline single-client synthetic (cold cache), scaled steady-state (warm cache with realistic concurrency), and burst stress (spikes). each phase will collect TTFT, TPOT, token-level latency, and tail percentiles p50/p95/p99.
[02:22] Leah: when you say cold vs warm cache, what exact state? can you enumerate?
[02:27] Connor: sure. cold cache = no KV/prefix cached and no warmed model artifacts; warm cache = warmed KV cache for common prefixes and model runtime warmed (JIT kernels loaded). we'll also instrument KV-hit rate and separate metrics for cold-first requests vs subsequent streamed tokens.
[02:45] Maya: we should define acceptance criteria per phase. proposal: Phase A baseline: TTFT p95 <= 160ms for short (<=64 token) replies; TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token for medium (<=256 token) outputs. Phase B steady: sustain 150 req/s with p95 TTFT <= 200ms and pipeline TPOT p95 <= 35ms. Phase C spikes: 10x burst for 30s, TTFT p99 shouldn't exceed 400ms and overall system degrades gracefully (fallback to smaller model).
[03:18] Carlos: hmm p99 400ms on bursts seems... ambitious but maybe fine with fallback. what's the fallback path?
[03:25] Connor: fallback is policy-driven: route to a cheaper model variant (e.g., quantized 8-bit) or route to dedicated spare pool. That'll be part of the test plan to validate automatic routing.
[03:36] Leah: can we measure cost per 1k tokens during these runs? need to compare to our budget.
[03:41] Maya: yes we'll capture token counts and per-token billing estimates with Redwood Optimize sim. we'll produce a cost delta sheet after baseline run.
[03:49] Sofia: on the study materials — leah will prepare a sample corpus of prompts and expected length distributions. we'll anonymize traces and send by monday.
[03:56] Carlos: also want to ensure p95 vs p99 — which do we gate on for acceptance? p95 feels OK for regular ops but execs will ask for p99 numbers.
[04:06] Connor: recommend dual gating: require p95 to be within target for acceptance and p99 to be within an upper bound (e.g., 2x p95) with a mitigation plan. if p99 is out of band we can run focused tail analysis.
[04:20] Maya: agreed. i'll note acceptance criteria: p95 pass + p99 mitigation plan requirement.
[04:27] [05:00] (small cross-talk, background noise)
[05:20] Connor: measurement details — we'll use synthetic drivers that replay real traces at time-of-day distributions: 60% short prompts (<64 tokens), 30% medium (64-256), 10% long (>256). batch sizes tested: 1, 4, 8. concurrency sweep up to 200 clients during steady-state.
[06:05] Leah: do you support custom model quantization during the POC? we want 4-bit/8-bit variants tested.
[06:11] Connor: yes we can test quantized variants. note performance tradeoffs: lower precision reduces TPOT but may raise serving memory and in some cases TTFT changes due to kernel selection. we'll document model variant matrix.
[06:28] Carlos: what's the plan for measuring exact TTFT? where are timestamps taken?
[06:33] Connor: TTFT measured at request ingestion (HTTP receive) to first token emit on the stream. we'll capture client-side and server-side views — client synthetic driver timestamps and agent-side trace. we expect small clock skew; we'll rely on server-side metric as canonical.
[06:50] Maya: include p95/p99 computed across the client-visible series and server-series. we will also surface per-route costs and token counts.
[07:01] Carlos: what about warmup windows? do you recommend a warmup period before measurement?
[07:06] Connor: always. recommended warmup 5-10 minutes depending on kernel JIT and KV cache. for large models with cold-start JIT it might be longer; we'll plan a staggered warmup then a 10-minute steady measurement window.
[07:22] Leah: timeline — how long will the POC take end-to-end?
[07:28] Maya: proposed timeline: week 0 (this week): sign-off and data share; week 1: infra & peering + Redwood harness set up; week 2: baseline and steady runs; week 3: spike tests, analysis & handoff. ~3 weeks.
[07:42] Carlos: that fits our schedule. can you show me the test matrix now?
[07:46] Connor: yes — live runbook (I'll paste link) — but verbally: axis one = model variant (full fp16, q8, q4), axis two = sequence length bucket, axis three = batch size. for each cell we collect TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, request success rate, KV hit rate, and per-token cost estimate.
[08:10] Leah: and for the acceptance gating — which cells matter most?
[08:14] Maya: we'll prioritize the short/interactive bucket and q8 variant first. if those pass we'll expand to medium and q4.
[08:23] Sofia: security question — we need audit logs and KMS integration tested during POC. does Redwood support bring-your-own-key on these environments?
[08:32] Connor: on private POC (customer VPC) yes — BYOK can be integrated, but it may add setup time. for initial perf bench we can run without BYOK, then verify BYOK flows in the last phase.
[08:45] Carlos: ok — that sequencing is ok. we need a SOC2/ISO doc as well.
[08:49] Maya: will send SOC2 summary in parallel.
[08:52] [09:30] (brief pause while links are pasted)
[10:05] Connor: important note on metrics collection: TTFT is sensitive to TLS handshake and network; we will attempt to colocate the client driver in the same region to minimize network noise. we'll run a few samples from external client too to approximate real user-experienced latency.
[10:28] Leah: good. for tokens per second — is TPOT linear with concurrency? at some point we see contention, right?
[10:34] Connor: yes non-linear at high concurrency, due to batching efficiency vs GPU utilization. that's why we sweep concurrency and batch sizes. the TPU/GPU kernels pick different code paths based on sequence length.
[10:48] Maya: another acceptance nuance — we will allow temporary tail increases during cache cold-start as long as the steady windows meet targets. that will be in the POC policy doc.
[11:00] Carlos: let's define clear pass/fail language: pass if all prioritized cells meet TTFT p95 targets and p99 is within 2x with documented mitigations. if fail, provide remediation tasks and rerun window.
[11:15] Maya: noted. we'll draft an acceptance checklist.
[11:21] Connor: instrumentation plan: we'll expose per-request traces, token-level latency histograms, GPU utilization, memory usage, and request routing logs. we'll also correlate KV-hit rates.
[11:34] Leah: can we get the raw histograms? our SRE will want them.
[11:38] Connor: yes we'll provide raw histograms and a dashboard link.
[11:42] Sofia: about cost — can you simulate per-customer cost for projected QPS? we have a cost target per 1M tokens per month.
[11:50] Maya: Redwood Optimize will give per-1k token cost estimates across model variants; we'll produce a cost projection doc as part of the POC report.
[12:00] Carlos: any gotchas you've seen in other customers for TTFT?
[12:06] Connor: common gotchas: (1) mixing very long and very short requests causes batching inefficiencies, (2) insufficient warmup, (3) incorrect pinning of model variants leading to unexpected kernel fallback. we will include checks for those.
[12:25] Leah: we use prefix-caching heavily for autocomplete — can you simulate high KV hit rates?
[12:30] Connor: yes tests will include controlled KV hit rates: 0%, 50%, 90% to show delta on TTFT and TPOT.
[12:40] [13:00] (short side conversation about infra windows)
[13:45] Maya: recap: agreed metrics (TTFT/TPOT/p95/p99), measurement phases, acceptance gating (p95 pass + p99 mitigation), timeline 3 weeks, and deliverables (benchmark harness, raw histograms, cost sheet, SOC2 summary).
[14:02] Carlos: next step — send the harness and we'll drop traces in S3 for you?
[14:06] Maya: yes send to the S3 share link we'll provide, we'll run tests from our harness or we can run them from your side depending on preference.
[14:14] Leah: one more Q: what about measuring noise from other tenants if we use Redwood hosted shared infra for the POC?
[14:20] Connor: we recommend dedicated pool for deterministic results; shared hosted can be used for a quick sanity check but results won't be gating. we'll note the environment in the report.
[14:32] Sofia: ok Palo Alto legal will need a data processing addendum if we transfer traces; we'll review.
[14:38] Maya: understood, legal review parallel track.
[14:42] (closing exchange)
[14:50] Carlos: thanks all. leaning positive. we'll try to get Leah's traces to you by monday and confirm the peering next thursday.
[14:58] Maya: great, i'll send the harness + acceptance checklist by saturday; Connor will share the matrix and runbook. thanks everyone.
[15:05] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker attribution errors: some short lines might be concatenated; filler words and small hesitations retained for realism.

Attachments referenced: Redwood benchmark harness (link above), preliminary acceptance checklist (to be sent), SOC2 summary (to be shared).
